title: 04 · Which graph?
summary: Let the variables choose the chart: histogram, scatterplot, boxplot, bar chart with the points, and a checklist for figures.
question: How do the types of your variables decide which graph to draw?

chain.title: Response, explanatory, continuous, categorical
chain.statement: The response (y axis) is the outcome you measure; the explanatory variable (x axis) is what might drive it; y ~ x reads "y as a function of x".

explain.text: A continuous variable is a scale (hours, kg); a categorical one is groups (flying yes/no, danger 1–5). Two questions pick the chart: how many variables, and of which kinds. One continuous → histogram; two continuous → scatterplot; continuous by groups → boxplot; a value per group → bars with the points.

terms.meaning: the measured outcome, on the y axis
the candidate cause or grouping, on the x axis
a measured scale / a set of groups

chain.intuition: y is the effect you watch, x the knob you suspect.

intuitionFigure.caption: x is the knob, y the dial.

chain.misconception: It does not matter which variable goes on which axis. Convention puts the response on y, which is how readers read cause and effect.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Response on y, explanatory on x.

check.q: Sleep hours against danger level 1–5: which graph?
check.a: A boxplot: a continuous response split by groups.

chain.opens: What graph shows the shape of one continuous variable?
chain.answers: How do the types of your variables decide which graph to draw?

chain.title: Histogram: the shape of one variable
chain.statement: hist(dat$TotalSleep) groups the values into intervals and draws touching bars whose heights count the species in each.

explain.text: The bars touch because x is a continuous scale with no gaps between intervals. Look at the shape before picking a test: one peak or two, symmetric or skewed. For sleep (2 to 20 hours, counts up to 12 species per bar) the shape decides between a t-test and a rank test later.

lines.explain: histogram of hours of sleep; R chooses the intervals

lines.code: hist(dat$TotalSleep, breaks = 10, xlab = "Total sleep (h per day)")
lines.explain: about 10 intervals and an axis label with units

code.interpret: Read the shape: centre, spread, skew, peaks.

terms.meaning: bars over adjacent intervals of a continuous variable; heights = counts
a long tail on one side

chain.intuition: A histogram is a pile of the data sorted into bins.

wrong.title: Mistaken
wrong.text: Gaps between bars of a histogram.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Bars touch: the scale is continuous.

chain.misconception: A histogram and a bar chart are the same. Bars of a bar chart stand for separate categories; a histogram's bins are adjacent intervals.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Histogram: intervals of a scale; bar chart: separate groups.

check.q: Why check the histogram before choosing a test?
check.a: A strongly skewed or two-peaked shape breaks the normality that t-tests assume; it points to a rank test.

chain.opens: How do you see whether two continuous variables are related?
chain.answers: What graph shows the shape of one continuous variable?

chain.title: Scatterplot: two continuous variables
chain.statement: plot(log10(dat$BodyWt), dat$TotalSleep) draws one dot per mammal; with body mass on a log axis the dots fall from upper left to lower right: bigger mammals sleep less (r = −0.53).

explain.text: Body mass runs from 0.005 to 6,654 kg, a factor of more than a million. On an ordinary axis nearly every dot would pile into the left corner. Taking log10 spaces the masses evenly by powers of ten (0.005 → −2.3, 6,654 → 3.8), so the pattern becomes visible: bats sleep long, the elephant short.

figure.caption: log10 spreads 0.005 kg to 6,654 kg evenly over powers of ten.

explain.text: The correlation r = −0.53 measures how tightly the dots follow a straight falling line: −1 would be a perfect line, 0 no linear pattern. A moderate negative value says the tendency is clear but individual mammals vary a lot.

lines.explain: x = log10 of body mass, y = hours of sleep; one dot per mammal
the correlation, ignoring rows with NAs

code.interpret: Larger mammals tend to sleep less; the relation is moderate, not tight.

terms.meaning: strength and direction of a linear relation, from −1 to 1

chain.intuition: A log axis is a zoom that treats a mouse and an elephant fairly.

intuitionFigure.caption: The trend of the sheet: down from bats to the elephant (dots sketch the direction only).

chain.misconception: r = −0.53 means body mass causes less sleep. Correlation in observational data does not show cause.

wrong.title: Mistaken
wrong.text: Heavier bodies make mammals sleep less.

right.title: Instead
right.text: They go together; predation risk or diet may drive both.

check.q: Without the log, where would most dots sit?
check.a: Squashed against the y axis: almost all mammals weigh far less than the largest ones.

wrong.title: Mistaken
wrong.text: Linear axis spreads the dots well.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Linear axis piles them in a corner.

chain.opens: How do you compare a continuous variable between groups?
chain.answers: How do you see whether two continuous variables are related?

chain.title: Boxplot: do groups differ?
chain.statement: boxplot(TotalSleep ~ Danger, data = dat) draws one box per danger level: the box is the middle 50% (the IQR), the thick line the median, whiskers reach the furthest point within 1.5 × IQR, dots beyond are outliers.

explain.text: Reading across the five danger levels (low → high) compares their medians and spreads at once. Mammals in high danger of predation sleep less, which fits the story of the scatterplot: big animals and prey animals sleep short.

figure.caption: Anatomy of one box (no data: what each part means).

lines.explain: formula: sleep (response) by danger (group); data = dat names the data frame

lines.code: boxplot(TotalSleep ~ Danger, data = dat, xlab = "Danger of predation", ylab = "Total sleep (h)")

code.interpret: Lower boxes at higher danger: animals at risk sleep less.

terms.meaning: interquartile range: the middle 50% of the values
a value beyond 1.5 × IQR from the box

chain.intuition: Each box is a histogram seen from above, squeezed to its five landmarks.
chain.misconception: The whiskers show the minimum and maximum. They stop at 1.5 × IQR; points beyond are drawn separately as outliers.

check.q: Two boxes overlap a lot but their medians differ. Does that prove a difference?
check.a: No: it suggests one; a test (sheet 06) decides how likely such a gap is by chance.

chain.opens: What is wrong with a bar of means, and how do you fix it?
chain.answers: How do you compare a continuous variable between groups?

chain.title: A value per group: bars plus the points
chain.statement: A bar of means hides the data: "flying" is just 2 bats against 56 non-flying mammals; draw the points and give n.

explain.text: barplot(means) shows two bars of similar height, which looks like a fair comparison. Adding the points with points() reveals that one bar rests on two animals and the other on 56: the flying mean is almost no evidence at all. Lecture 5 calls bars of means without data "dynamite plots".

figure.caption: How many animals stand behind each bar.

lines.code: means <- tapply(dat$TotalSleep, dat$Flying, mean, na.rm = TRUE)

lines.explain: draw the bars; b holds their x positions
add every animal as a dot over its bar

code.interpret: The dots show the n behind each mean.

terms.meaning: the number of observations in a group
a bar of means with an error bar and no data

chain.intuition: A bar is a promise; the points are the evidence.

right.title: Instead
right.text: One bar is 2 bats, the other 56 mammals.

chain.misconception: Bars of equal height mean equally reliable groups.

right.title: Instead
right.text: n = 2 versus n = 56: very different certainty.

check.q: What two things should a group comparison figure always show?
check.a: The data points (or their spread) and n per group.

chain.opens: What must a figure have before you hand it in?
chain.answers: What is wrong with a bar of means, and how do you fix it?

chain.title: Before you hand in a figure
chain.statement: Nine checks: response on y, explanatory on x; axis labels with units; log() if squashed; show the data, not just means; no 3-D or chartjunk; bars start at zero; a legend for groups; colour-blind-safe colours plus pch shapes; a caption saying what, n and colours.

explain.text: Pie or donut charts only suit parts of a whole and people judge angles badly, so a bar chart is usually clearer; never use 3-D. Bars encode values by length, so they must start at zero; colours alone fail for colour-blind readers, so pair them with point shapes (pch).

terms.meaning: decoration that carries no data (shadows, 3-D, textures)
plotting character: the point symbol in R

chain.intuition: A figure is an argument: every mark must carry evidence.

right.title: Instead
right.text: Labelled bars from zero with points.

chain.misconception: Truncating the y axis makes small differences visible, so it is fine for bars. For bars it exaggerates: length must be proportional to value.

wrong.title: Mistaken
wrong.text: Start bars at 9 h to show the gap.

check.q: Why add pch shapes when you already use colours?
check.a: About 1 in 12 men is colour-blind; shapes keep the groups distinguishable.
